title: Let Your Characters Shine

title: Let Players Cheat the System

title: Long Ago, Numbers Were Used to Draw Pixel Art

takeaways: Early microcomputer pixel art was entered as hex numbers; One hex digit encodes a 4x1 pixel strip; Two stacked bit layers give three colors plus transparency; Run compression: 0x8 instead of 00000000; Easy input today, but far more complex graphics

title: Dealing With Color Disparity
summary: Different monitors and room lighting change how color looks, so give your team a process for matching colors: a shared reference screen, calibration by eye and neutral lighting, so art isn't judged on screens that are lying.
takeaways: Even identical monitors vary in color and brightness; Color variance is critical for artists and supervisors; Calibrate by sight against a shared, visible monitor; Some monitor gaps can't be calibrated away; Use neutral lighting; tinted rooms skew the art
tags: color calibration monitors lighting hardware team-workflow feedback-giving

title: Giving Feedback for Sound Effects
summary: Sound is hard to describe, so give sound designers concrete descriptions of a sound's role, comparisons everyone knows and links to real examples, then approve whatever fits the game even if it isn't what you first imagined.
takeaways: Audio feedback is hard; it has no physical form; Use concrete phrases and widely known comparisons; Attach links to real sound examples; Onomatopoeia alone fails in text, but adds clues; Approve sounds that fit the game, not your image

title: Show the Actual Game!
summary: Every game you sell needs a trailer, and that trailer should get to real gameplay as fast as possible, not spend its opening on logos, cinematics and story.
takeaways: A gameplay trailer is absolutely essential for selling; Get to actual gameplay as soon as possible; New IP and indie titles can't rely on teasers; Story and world can come later; Presentations are all about speed

title: Staying True to Your Concept
summary: Fix a clear concept before production starts and steer by it like a lighthouse for the whole project. Bring out emergent fun along the way, but don't change direction midway, or you'll waste your team's work and get lost.
takeaways: The concept gives a game its appeal and direction; Never change direction midway through development; Bring out emergent fun, but stay on course; Scrapping work wastes months and demotivates the team; Design docs can't fully convey a game's fun

title: Faithfulness Comes First in Licensed Games
summary: In a licensed game, faithfulness to the source and satisfying fans' love for it come first and fun comes second, so look for source settings that naturally become gameplay and use the gaps the source leaves to invent.
takeaways: Source material restricts licensed game design; Fans want faithfulness first, fun second; It's product value versus fun; Some settings map perfectly to gameplay; Freedom comes where the source shows little

title: Randomness Spices Games Up
summary: Use randomness to keep repeated play fresh and make players adapt, but never let luck alone decide a loss, keep it out of strict skill contests, and seed it so players can't manipulate it.
takeaways: Randomness keeps repeated play fresh; It adds strategy by forcing adaptation; Players must feel responsible for their own failure; Keep randomness out of strict skill competitions; Seed randomness with the clock to prevent manipulation

title: Turning Gift-Giving Into a Game
summary: When you have things to give your team, turn the giveaway into a small game: it works as an icebreaker and builds the kind of director–team relationship game development should have.
takeaways: Give spare games and hardware to the team; Run giveaways as a sign-up lottery; Decide winners with games, sometimes with secret rules; Fun giveaways act as team icebreakers; Good director–team relationships are how dev should be
tags: team-culture motivation direction communication party-game kirby smash-bros

title: Don’t Put Decisions Off
summary: Make decisions on the spot instead of saying "later", because every minute of waiting leaves the team blocked, but stay flexible enough to correct a call once you see it was wrong.
takeaways: Don't end meetings with 'I'll decide later'; Push whoever has authority to decide now; Every minute of waiting leaves issues unresolved; Give deciders accurate, reliable information; Stay flexible; correct mistakes with slight adjustments

title: Motion Blur
summary: Use blur to show motion and fill the gaps between frames, through drawn blur textures or hardware effects, but keep it subtle and natural (or let players adjust it), because too much blur makes the action hard to read.
takeaways: Blur shows afterimages and fills gaps between frames; Swap in blurred textures for spinning objects; Blur can be hand-drawn or hardware-calculated; Don't overdo it; fuzzy visuals hide the action; Offer a blur-strength option

title: Game Essence in Action Games
summary: Every action-game verb (jumping, dashing, melee, shooting, dodging, parrying, hiding) should pair a danger with an opportunity, so understand why each one's risk and reward works instead of just copying it.
takeaways: Game essence is taking risks and earning rewards; Every action pairs danger with opportunity; Parrying turns massive risk into massive reward; Longer range weapons often come with less ammo; Understand the meaning; go beyond mere imitation

title: Animation Blending
summary: Blend between animations so transitions such as cancels look natural from any starting pose, but keep blends short and snappy, because long automatic blends kill rhythm and impact and can distort the motion.
takeaways: Blending combines two or more animations; Cancels blend into the next action, not snap; Too-smooth blends lose rhythm and impact; Keep blends quick and snappy; Blending shines most in fully 3D games

title: Debug Mode
summary: Give your team a well-organized debug mode, built into the normal controller through button combinations, because it's used every day and has a huge effect on productivity even though it's stripped from the final game.
takeaways: Debug mode tests and analyzes the game during development; Missing debug features force time-wasting workarounds; Some debug tools can become player features; Put debug controls on the gameplay controller; Keep debug modes organized and pruned

title: Crafting “Similar” Games
summary: It's fine to start by imitating a game you admire, but by the end of development your game needs many kinds of appeal the original lacks, or players will just play the original.
takeaways: Making similar games refined the industry; it's good; Any finished game beats no game; Players may just stick with the original; An homage needs many appeals the original lacks; Make something players can't get anywhere else

title: Button Settings
summary: Every game, however simple, should let players reassign buttons, ideally through a graphical controller screen, cursor-based assignment, shared actions and saveable profiles.
takeaways: Every game should have a key config; Show controllers graphically, not as vertical lists; Assign with cursor, not press-to-assign; Let multiple buttons share one action; Save layouts to profiles, even on the controller

title: Competition and Abundance
summary: If you release games commercially, treat every game players could spend their hours on, new or old, as your competition, and let gratitude for that abundance fuel your work.
takeaways: You compete for players' hours against every game ever made; Subscription services pit new releases against back catalogs; Player abundance exists because creators braved the competition; Making games deepens your understanding of why games are fun

title: A World Without Footprints
summary: Every now and then, play a game completely blind, with no trailers, spoilers, strategy guides or Let's Plays, because it lets you feel more and it is the best way to study someone else's work.
takeaways: Occasionally play games completely blind, avoiding all spoilers; Skip trailers, guides and Let's Plays until finished; Form your own impressions before reading others' opinions; Blind play is the best way to study others' work

title: Presenting Scores
summary: Don't take the score for granted: give it a meaningful unit of measurement, such as an age, money or a power rating, and present each increase so that earning it feels great.
takeaways: Never take the score for granted; design its presentation; Express scores in a meaningful unit of measurement; Concrete units like money make the experience feel real; Count score increases up point by point

title: Making Effects the Right Size
summary: Give effects enough density to match the world's scale: a large flame needs many loops or small, detailed particles, or it will read as a candle.
takeaways: Effects must match the world's sense of scale; Big flames lacking density look like candles; Add loops or smaller, detailed particles for density; Effects move constantly; make them quick and fierce, not detailed

title: Handicap Systems
summary: Decide on purpose how much your competitive game should even out skill: casual games need catch-up systems so everyone gets turns winning, while a game meant to reflect skill should limit leveling to chaotic elements and optional settings.
takeaways: Casual games need catch-up systems so everyone wins sometimes; Skill-focused games shouldn't buff trailing players' stats; Route catch-up through chaos: items, stages, comeback meters; Human adjustments are the most effective handicap

title: Making "Work" Games Fun
summary: A game with little push-and-pull can still hook players if it simulates real-world work, runs a work-earn-upgrade loop and keeps the ending out of sight.
takeaways: Fun can exist without push-and-pull or risk; Base work games on real-world tasks players can imagine; Design the work-earn-upgrade loop first; Hide the ending far away if there isn't one

title: Balancing Ambient Sounds
summary: Mix ambient sounds at the lowest priority so they never mask important effects, but don't cut them, because quiet, fairly realistic ambience is what makes the game world feel real.
takeaways: Ambient sounds take the lowest mix priority; Never let ambience mask important sound effects; Dead silence kills atmosphere; always layer ambience; Use realistic ambience even in cartoony games

title: Making the Imaginary Feel Real
summary: A game world is a massless mirage, so control every asset's texture, response to light, weight, use and placement, along with invisible things like airflow, until the world feels real.
takeaways: Game worlds are massless mirages; expression makes them feel real; Control texture, light, weight, use and placement of assets; Presentation and arrangement decide whether objects feel real; Simulate invisible forces like wind and explosion gusts

title: Using Parameters to Establish Characters
summary: Start each character from a neutral, workable baseline, then push their parameters and unique mechanics far enough that their identity fits in a word or two, and budget the programming that takes.
takeaways: Start neutral, then deviate boldly for each character; Describe each character's identity in a word or two; Unique mechanics require dedicated programming; budget for it; Emphasize parameter differences; fix issues during production

title: Playing Games in Front of Other People
summary: When you demo your game, plan your play so it shows as much of the content as possible in close matches, and imagine presenting your work even if you never will, because doing so organizes your thinking.
takeaways: Showing a game directly is the most effective presentation; Demo every special move and the super move; Keep demo matches relatively close; Imagining a presentation organizes your thoughts and reveals insights

title: Bug Testing Systems
summary: Run bug testing as a dedicated, ticket-driven system (latest daily build, systematic coverage, severity classes, routing to whoever can fix it, tickets kept as resolved), because every fix can create a new bug.
takeaways: Use dedicated bug testers, not programmers, for testing; Everyone tests the latest daily build; Track reproducible bugs as severity-classed tickets routed to owners; Keep fixed tickets resolved, never discarded; Every fix risks new bugs; find and fix fast

title: Portraying Fingers
summary: Angle the fingers in a diagonal grip on anything swung with the forearm so it looks natural, and spend finger bones and processing only where they matter.
takeaways: Use a diagonal grip for objects swung with the forearm; Perpendicular grips make characters look like action figures; Fingers are the first thing cut under processing load; Swap pre-made finger patterns instead of full articulation

title: Advancing Text
summary: Let players get through text and dialogue at their own, usually fast, pace, with line-by-line skipping in cutscenes or voiced lines they can hear while playing, because modern players want to enjoy as much as possible in as little time as possible.
takeaways: Players read fast; let them zip through text; Offer line-by-line skipping in voiced cutscenes; Let players hear dialogue while they keep playing; Modern audiences want maximum enjoyment in minimum time

title: Say It, and It Might Come True
summary: The words you use shape your attitude and your actions, so stop broadcasting defeatist thoughts, turn negative feelings into concrete questions about how to improve, and take on challenges fired up.
takeaways: Your words shape your attitude and actions; Avoid voicing defeatist thoughts, especially on social media; Turn negative feelings into questions about improvement; Meet challenges head-on and psych yourself up

title: Better Than Not Being Able to Beat the Game
summary: Always give stuck players a way forward, such as changing difficulty at any time or skipping after repeated failure, because once a player gives up, your challenge is worth nothing.
takeaways: Never let players hit an unbeatable wall; Let difficulty change anytime without restarting; Offer easier modes or skips after repeated failure; Help players without humiliating them; Hardcore design is valid but not for everyone

title: A World with Less Color
summary: If gameplay depends on telling colors apart, check it through a color-blindness filter and separate similar hues by brightness, and check your art in black and white so backgrounds never outshine the foreground.
takeaways: Never rely solely on color for gameplay distinctions; Check visuals with a color-blindness filter; Separate similar hues with strong brightness differences; Check art in black and white for value balance; Backgrounds shouldn't outshine the foreground

title: Final Output
summary: On powerful hardware, judge visuals by the final composited frame (post-processing, blended hues, reflections) rather than by individually polished models, and consider giving post-processing its own specialist.
takeaways: On modern hardware, final output matters more than ever; Post-processing in the framebuffer drives graphical quality; Judge how everything comes together, not individual models; Teams will want dedicated post-processing specialists

title: Storage Tips
summary: Keep your reference library of games, consoles, controllers and cables organized and quick to reach, because for a developer old games remain working tools.
takeaways: Keep reference games and hardware organized and accessible; One switchable cabinet gives quick access to many consoles; Label every cable and adapter; Old games stay useful as work reference and footage

title: Transparency Features
summary: Add developer-mode tools that make chosen parts of a model translucent or invisible, and that toggle each display element on or off, so animations and screens can be checked without obstruction.

title: Average and Mediocre Are the Same Thing
summary: When balancing, keep characters distinctive by amplifying their shortcomings to offset their strengths, not by sanding their strengths down, because average is mediocre.

title: Mandatory Strategies and Strategic Balance
summary: Choose deliberately where your encounters fall between authored, mandatory strategies and free-form approaches, based on your own game's systems rather than copying another game's answer.
takeaways: Authored boss strategies feel like tutorials but show care; Free-form strategies give freedom but less push and pull; Choose the strategic experience your game needs; Derive balance from your systems, not a reference game

title: Play Testing Keeps Going
summary: Rely on dedicated play testers, and on online match data where you have it, to tune balance, while the director steps in mainly to protect each character's individuality.

title: Computer-Controlled Players
summary: Build CPU opponents from data on reach, timing and the opponent's state, give them human-like reaction limits, and tune them to be fun (aggressive and beatable) rather than flawless.

title: Using Other Songs for Audio Reference
summary: Give your composer a concrete existing song as a starting point, but don't let you or them get fixated on it, because a new piece has to do more than imitate the reference.
takeaways: Concrete reference tracks give composers a clear starting point; Say which qualities of the reference to keep and drop; Fixating on one reference produces cheap imitations; License an existing song if it fits perfectly

title: Flashing Effects
summary: Use brief full-screen flashes for impact and character flashes to show status changes, and build dark elements into character flashes so they keep their contrast instead of fading into the background.
takeaways: Full-screen flashes add impact like screen shake; Character flashes emphasize status changes; Plain white flashes lose contrast on light backgrounds; Add shadows to flashes for internal contrast; Scale flash strength with camera distance

title: All to Destroy One Wall
summary: When supervising art, give precise, drawn feedback until an asset clearly reads as what it should be, and when repeated rounds still fall short, accept it and move on.
takeaways: Give art feedback with retouched reference images; Even spacing and copy-paste make breaks look fake; Judge assets by their core goal, not your mental image; Ship it as-is when repeated feedback stops converging

title: Always Keep Attack Collision in Mind
summary: Animators must always know when and where an attack's collision is active, so the animation lines up with the hitbox and the strongest pose lands on the hit frame.
takeaways: Fast games need hitboxes wider than the weapon; Attacks must cross the line where opponents stand; Start collision when the pose looks strongest; Animators share responsibility for game feel

title: Targeting and Market Research
summary: Don't let targeting and market research generate your new game ideas: they only describe paths others have already taken, and following them leads to average games in crowded markets.
takeaways: Market data describes the past, not what comes next; Audience boundaries by age and gender are blurry; Target "beginners", not a specific age range; Following the main road yields mediocre, lower-selling games

title: Gameplay as Part of a Live Performance
summary: Live, one-time stakes, such as a real chance of failing in front of an audience, are what make a gameplay performance thrilling and memorable.

title: Echo Chambers
summary: Notice when you're only hearing agreement about your ideas, designs or reviews, and stay objective, while still keeping the conviction to push your game in its own deliberately "unbalanced" direction.
takeaways: Agreement online reinforces views while dissenters stay unseen; Echo chambers affect design ideas and reviews daily; Without objectivity, a game ends up unbalanced; A deliberate unique direction still beats being swayed

title: Adding Help Text to Menus
summary: Add help text to menu items, write it in different words than the item's name, and trim it until its meaning is clear at a glance.
takeaways: Add help text to every menu item; Never explain an option using its own name; Cut excess words; translate meaning, not words; Avoid jargon like "config" or "key repeat"

title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
summary: In strategy games, start from symmetric fairness, then build push and pull through counters, costs, abilities and range, so the fun comes from out-configuring an evenly matched opponent.

title: Online Updates
summary: Treat post-launch patches as a bonus, not a plan: modern games will ship with bugs that only the market finds, but no patch helps once players have given up, so ship in the best shape you can.

title: Manga-like Visuals
summary: Borrow manga and anime's non-realistic conventions, like putting the mouth on the side of the face in profile, whenever they express a character better than realism would.

title: In-Game Cutscenes
summary: Use cutscenes where they add emotion, clarity or a breather, but respect the player's time: keep them tight, always let players skip them (credits included), ideally add fast-forward, and use quick-time events with great caution.

title: Directors and Producers
summary: Give a project one director who owns the content and concept, and a producer who owns money, staffing and marketing, and make sure both are working toward the same quality goal.

title: Start with the Climax

summary: Don't let convenient tools like realistic skeleton rigs decide what your animation can do; great animation goes beyond real-world limits.

title: When Ideas Won't Come
summary: When you're stuck for an idea, define the theme of the problem first, then generate as many candidate solutions as you can, following each thread before you prune.

title: How Good Were the Player’s Actions?
summary: Set difficulty, rewards and penalties by asking how good or bad the player's action really was, so consequences feel earned, while leaving room for deliberate surprises.

title: Turning Anything Into a Competitive Game

title: Being Kind to Beginners

summary: Establish a character with an exaggerated, readable silhouette and strong poses, and make sure everyone working on them understands the character's core essence and pushes it further.

title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!

title: Amplify Both Strengths and Weaknesses

title: Never Get Into Fights
summary: Treat every coworker as someone you'll work with again: never fight, badmouth people or leave on bad terms, because the game industry is small and that behavior comes back to you.
takeaways: The game industry is small; colleagues reappear years later; Never fight, badmouth, or leave on bad terms; Give constructive feedback openly; distance yourself if needed; Focus on supportive teammates, not unpleasant ones

title: Be Mindful of the Time Players are Giving You
summary: Treat play time as a cost the player pays, not a selling point: build the fun first, let long play time follow from it, and keep the player in control for as much of that time as possible.
takeaways: Advertised play time feels like a cost, not a perk; Games compete with everything else for players' time; Build fun first; let play time follow; Maximize the time players spend in control

title: Rotation on Two Axes
summary: When you animate anything that isn't a machine, never rotate on a single axis: pair the main turn with a second axis, move the connected joints, and hand-tune the timing so the motion looks believable and has personality.
takeaways: Single-axis rotation looks mechanical; combine two axes; Move shoulder and collarbone with a twisting wrist; Hand-tune curves: offset axes, add counter-motion; Plan head turns together with eye movement

title: CRT Displays
summary: Games are built for the screens they're shown on, and older games were made for CRTs (fast response, bright phosphors, light-gun timing, interlacing and hidden screen edges), so account for that hardware when you study, port or imitate them.
takeaways: Retro games were designed solely for CRT displays; CRTs respond fast; score-chasers still seek them out; Light guns relied on CRT scanline timing; Only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising: Sora Edition
summary: Quality comes from relentless, specific polish passes, so check poses, follow-through, effect readability, contrast and both versions of every move, and flag even tiny flaws with visual paintovers as soon as you see them.
takeaways: Check special moves in both ground and aerial versions; Bright-only effects vanish on bright stages; mix in dark; Foreground contrast strong, background contrast weak; Give feedback with paintovers; flag tiny flaws immediately; Polishing without fail is what raises quality

title: HUDs
summary: Design your HUD to be both easy and fun to use, keeping useful information on screen while finding tricks so it doesn't crowd the play area.
takeaways: HUDs are useful but crowd the screen; balance both; Auto-hide cursors by distance and situation; Make HUD semi-transparent when characters overlap it; Use HUD portraits and motion to add character appeal; Make meters react to game state

title: What Happens When You Shift the Center of Gravity?
summary: Don't settle for perfectly straight motion or rotation around an exact center: add a wobble to trajectories and move pivots off-center so objects move with personality instead of following your software's bland defaults.
takeaways: Straight lines and center-point spins look mechanical; Add a looping positional wobble to projectiles; Offset rotation axes from the object's center; Don't just follow your software's tendencies
games: Kirby series; Super Smash Bros. Ultimate

title: Give Yourself a Handicap When Balancing Your Game
summary: Developers know their game too well to be the difficulty standard, so tune difficulty while handicapping yourself (one hand, less health, stricter conditions) and then make it easier than you think it should be.
takeaways: Developers know the game too well to set difficulty; Balancing to the best staff player locks buyers out; Handicap yourself: one hand, lower health, stricter rules; Make it easier than you think it should be

title: No Masterpiece Has Bad Audio
summary: Treat music and sound effects as essential rather than secondary, because audio is what players remember first and what hits them in the heart, and no masterpiece has bad audio.
takeaways: No masterpiece has bad audio; Music and SFX are often what players remember first; Even simple noise effects can be well constructed; Good audio boosts enjoyment when players can listen

title: A Director’s Job is to Trim
summary: A director creates and also trims, cutting excess and steering the project back on course when plans slip, and that only works if team members report accurate information, including trouble, as early as possible.
takeaways: Directors trim excess, not just create; Course corrections are faster when the director leads them; Report trouble early with accurate information; Build teams where the baton passes quickly

title: Mr. Iwata
summary: Lead the way Sakurai remembers Satoru Iwata leading: trust creators with their content, step in personally when problems arise, meet trouble with calm logic instead of temper, and invest in direct, one-on-one communication.
takeaways: Trust creators with content; help when problems arise; Buggy code can't be fixed by tuning parameters; Stay calm and analytical where others lose their temper; Value one-on-one communication with your people; Names carry nuance: "Brothers" meant friends settling a disagreement

title: Up is Down, and Down is Up
summary: A leader isn't above the team: a director's instructions flow downstream, but they are really requests made from the bottom up to the people doing the work, so treat everyone with respect and as an ally.
takeaways: Leaders make requests from the bottom up; Nobody on the team is higher or lower; Nobody likes a demanding customer; show respect; Teammates are allies even when you disagree

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: Finale Special
summary: When you take on a big creative project next to your main job, plan and script all of it up front, prove it with a pilot, favor speed and brevity over perfection, clear reviews the day they arrive, and remember that shared knowledge only has meaning when people use it.
takeaways: Plan all content up front when juggling two big projects; Test feasibility with a finished pilot first; Short and snappy: speed above all else; Clear reviews the same day; set delivery cutoffs; Knowledge only has meaning when people use it
